{"claims": [
{"id": "c1", "text": "Stochastic Token Steering (STS) gates the SAE steering vector at each token with an independent Bernoulli(p) draw. In expectation a fraction p of positions is steered. p interpolates between no steering (p=0) and full steering (p=1). The method needs no reward model, learned selector, or auxiliary model during decoding.", "sections": ["s1", "s3", "s2", "s7"], "depends_on": []},
{"id": "c2", "text": "Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws one Bernoulli(p) gate per sequence and, if the gate fires, steers only a leading window of W positions. This relies on the disproportionate influence of early tokens. As a result, SBS realizes a much smaller and bounded fraction of steered tokens than STS at the same nominal p.", "sections": ["s3", "s10"], "depends_on": ["c1"]},
{"id": "c3", "text": "The steering direction comes from a pretrained SAE. Features are ranked by their mean activation difference between a behavior-positive set and a neutral set. The decoder directions of the top-K features are summed and normalized to unit norm, so the magnitude alpha alone sets intervention strength.", "sections": ["s3", "s9", "s6"], "depends_on": []},
{"id": "c4", "text": "Sparse STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect. On LLaMA it recovers over 95% of the toxicity reduction at p=0.5 and over 75% of the emotion gains by p=0.7. It also surpasses a deliberately strong engineered prompting baseline in 5 of 6 model-task settings, though the ratio needed is task dependent.", "sections": ["s4", "s8", "s10"], "depends_on": ["c1", "c8"]},
{"id": "c5", "text": "Fluency degradation (perplexity, repetition) rises monotonically with steering density, so sparse operating points cost less fluency than full steering. Separately, lightweight guards (norm preservation, clamping, repetition penalty) are needed to keep generation on-manifold.", "sections": ["s4", "s7", "s9"], "depends_on": ["c1"]},
{"id": "c6", "text": "At matched nominal p, STS produces a larger behavioral shift than SBS. Much of this gap reflects SBS's smaller realized budget. At matched realized budgets no single ordering holds: STS keeps an edge on toxicity, while SBS is competitive on fear.", "sections": ["s4", "s10", "s7"], "depends_on": ["c2", "c4"]},
{"id": "c7", "text": "The best-performing steering magnitude alpha* rises as the intervention ratio p falls. Both alpha and p increase residual-stream displacement: p adds displaced positions, while alpha deepens displacement per token. They therefore act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift.", "sections": ["s4", "s10", "s5"], "depends_on": ["c1"]},
{"id": "c8", "text": "Alpha is calibrated once per model and task under full steering (p=1), at the point that maximizes effect just before fluency sharply degrades. It is then held fixed across all methods and ratios, so the sparse results get no per-p magnitude re-tuning.", "sections": ["s4", "s10"], "depends_on": ["c3"]}
],
"items": [
{"id": "q1", "claim": "c1", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s9"], "question": "A user runs STS with p=0.25 and generates the paper's maximum of 128 tokens. How many generated positions should they expect to receive the steering vector, and why?", "answer": "About 32 positions (0.25 × 128). Each position's gate is an independent Bernoulli(0.25) draw, so the expected number steered is p times the number of positions.", "rubric": ["States approximately 32 positions", "Explains that each token is gated independently with probability p, so the expected count is p × length"]},

How would the steering of a single generation differ from the paper's STS, even though the expected fraction of steered tokens is still p?", "answer": "Each generation would be either fully steered or not steered at all, rather than having a random subset of its tokens steered. The paper's STS uses i.i.d. per-token gates, which spread steering across positions within every sequence. The altered version would amount to SBS with a window covering the whole sequence.", "rubric": ["States that each generation becomes all-or-nothing (fully steered with probability p, otherwise unsteered)", "Contrasts this with STS's independent per-token gates, which steer a partial subset within each sequence"]},
{"id": "q3", "claim": "c1", "kind": "claim", "form": "spot-wrong-version", "level": "textbase", "sections": ["s2", "s3", "s7"], "question": "A reviewer summarizes STS as 'like SIA, it identifies the behaviorally critical token positions and steers only those.' Why is this summary wrong according to the paper?", "answer": "STS does not identify critical positions. Its gates are random i.i.d. Bernoulli draws that make no assumption about which tokens matter, and no learned value model or selector is involved. SIA, by contrast, uses entropy and a trained value model to choose positions.", "rubric": ["States that STS selects positions at random rather than choosing critical tokens", "Notes that STS uses no learned selector or value model, unlike SIA"]},
{"id": "q4", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s10"], "question": "In the paper's Table 1, SBS at p=0.5 has a realized ratio of 0.134 with W=32 and 0.261 with W=64. What feature of SBS's definition explains why doubling W roughly doubles the realized ratio?", "answer": "When the single gate fires, exactly the first W positions are steered and none after. Doubling W therefore doubles the number of tokens steered per firing, while the firing probability p stays the same. The fraction of steered tokens thus scales roughly with W.", "rubric": ["Identifies that a firing gate steers exactly W leading positions and nothing beyond", "Concludes that steered tokens per sequence, and hence the realized ratio, scale roughly in proportion to W at fixed p"]},
{"id": "q5", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s10"], "question": "Even with p set to 1, would SBS with W=64 steer every token of a sequence longer than 64 tokens? Explain using the method's definition.", "answer": "No. SBS only ever adds the steering vector at positions t ≤ W, and positions beyond the window are left unperturbed. So even at p=1 its realized ratio stays below 1 for longer sequences, unlike STS, which reaches full steering at p=1.", "rubric": ["Concludes that not all tokens would be steered (realized ratio stays below 1)", "Explains that positions after the window W are never steered under SBS"]},
{"id": "q6", "claim": "c2", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s1"], "question": "SBS is motivated by prior findings about early tokens. SBS steers only the leading window on the premise that early-token intervention disproportionately shapes later behavior. Without that influence, steering a short leading window would be expected to have little effect on the rest of the generation.", "rubric": ["States that SBS's justification would be undermined, so weak effects would be expected", "Explains that SBS steers only the leading window, relying on early tokens' outsized influence"]},
{"id": "q7", "claim": "c3", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3"], "question": "An SAE feature has mean activation 0.8 on the neutral set and 0.2 on the positive (target-behavior) set. Would the paper's discovery procedure include it among the top-K steering features? Why?", "answer": "No. Its differential Δ = 0.2 − 0.8 = −0.6 is negative. The procedure selects the features with the largest Δ, meaning those more active on the positive set, so this feature would rank near the bottom.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the feature would not be selected", "Computes or reasons that Δ (positive minus neutral) is negative, and selection takes the top features by Δ"]},
{"id": "q8", "claim": "c3", "kind": "claim", "form": "change-condition", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s10"], "question": "The paper normalizes the summed SAE decoder directions to unit norm. Alpha would then no longer be the sole control of intervention strength, and calibrated values would not carry over. {"id": "q9", "claim": "c3", "kind": "claim", "form": "connect-sections", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s3", "s6"], "question": "The Limitations section says steering quality depends on the choice of contrastive corpora. Which step of the method creates this dependence?", "answer": "The feature-selection step creates it. Features are ranked by Δ, the difference in mean activation between the positive set and the neutral control set. If these sets are poorly matched, the top-Δ features may reflect incidental differences rather than the target behavior, giving a poor steering direction.", "rubric": ["Identifies the mean activation differential (Δ) computed from the positive and neutral sets as the source", "Explains that poorly chosen sets would select features unrelated to the target behavior"]},

{"id": "q13", "claim": "c5", "kind": "claim", "form": "apply-new-case", "level": "situation", "sections": ["s4"], "question": "A practitioner considers using STS at p=0.4 instead of full steering for toxicity reduction on Gemma-2 2B. ANSWER Q1: The paper's contrastive corpora dependence is introduced in step 2 of the method, where it describes how the SAE is trained on residual-stream activations at a single intermediate layer. This step creates a dependence on the choice of contrastive corpora.

ANSWER Q2: The paper's residual-stream displacement analysis explains that increasing steering strength (α) deepens the displacement at each intervened token, while increasing the fraction of steered tokens (p) adds more displaced positions. This means that as p falls, the displacement increases, but the effect of α remains the same.

ANSWER Q3: The paper's discovery procedure would include the SAE feature with mean activation 0.2 on the positive set, because the difference between the mean activation on the positive set and the neutral set is large enough to make it a candidate for the top-K steering features.

ANSWER Q4: The paper declines to put SIA's reported numbers side by side because SIA is a reward-guided method, whereas STS is a sparse activation steering method that uses a fixed steering direction and an independent Bernoulli(p) draw per token. The paper wants to make a direct comparison between the two methods' effectiveness.

ANSWER Q5: The user cannot reuse LLaMA 3.1-8B's calibrated toxicity alpha (2) for Gemma-2 2B because the two models are from different families and the calibration was done at p=1, not p=0.5.

ANSWER Q6: The reported sparse-steering recovery numbers are likely optimistic because the experiments were run with alpha fixed at its p=1 calibrated value, while the alpha–p interaction in Section 4.3 suggests that the optimal alpha may differ at lower values of p.

ANSWER Q7: The alpha at p=0.3 is likely too high because the paper's alpha–p finding suggests that the optimal alpha decreases as p increases.

ANSWER Q8: The paper's protocol rules out the possibility that STS looks good at low p only because of the way it searches for the best steering magnitude separately at each p. The paper finds the optimal alpha for each p and uses it to evaluate STS.

ANSWER Q9: Lowering p helps fluency because it reduces the number of steered tokens, which reduces the overall impact of the steering signal on the model's generation.

ANSWER Q10: The comparison shows that SBS steers more tokens at p=0.5 (0.261) than STS (0.492), but the increase in the realized ratio is not directly related to the difference in steering tokens. Instead, the comparison suggests that SBS's definition allows it to steer a larger fraction of tokens at p=0.5.

ANSWER Q11: STS is more disadvantaged by the fixed alpha at p=0.5 because it steers a larger fraction of tokens (49%) than SBS (13%), but the paper's alpha–p finding suggests that STS is more effective at lower values of p.

ANSWER Q12: The comparison suggests that STS retains a toxicity advantage at matched nominal p because its realized ratio (0.492) is higher than SBS's (0.261) at p=0.5.

ANSWER Q13: The reviewer's summary is wrong because STS identifies behaviorally critical token positions and steers only those, whereas SIA steers only at position-based gates.

ANSWER Q14: If STS were altered to decide the gate for all tokens with a single Bernoulli(p) draw per sequence, the steering of a single generation would differ from the paper's STS because the expected fraction of steered tokens would be the same, but the actual fraction steered would be the same as well.

ANSWER Q15: If the paper had picked an alpha well beyond the inflection, the full-steering baseline would have looked worse, because the optimal alpha would have been at a higher value than the one used.

ANSWER Q16: Normalizing the summed SAE decoder directions to unit norm does not change the meaning of a given alpha value, because the paper normalizes the steering direction to ensure that it is a unit vector.

ANSWER Q17: If the fluency-preserving guards were turned off, the ablation would suggest that perplexity on the Gemma-2 2B toxicity setting would be higher because the steering signal would have a greater impact on the model's generation.

ANSWER Q18: If full steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B reduced mean toxicity by 0.30, STS at p=0.5 would likely achieve a toxicity reduction of around 0.20, because the paper's alpha–p finding suggests that the optimal alpha decreases as p increases.

ANSWER Q19: SBS with W=64 would steer every token of a sequence longer than 64 tokens because its definition allows it to steer a leading window of size W.

ANSWER Q20: The comparison shows that SBS (W=64) at p=0.5 has a higher realized ratio (0.261) and lower gain (0.092) than STS (p=0.5) (0.492 and 0.237), indicating that SBS is less effective at steering.

ANSWER Q21: SBS is more disadvantaged by the fixed alpha at p=0.5 because it steers a smaller fraction of tokens (13%) than STS (49%).

ANSWER Q22: The comparison shows that STS retains a toxicity advantage at matched nominal p because its realized ratio (0.492) is higher than SBS's (0.261) at p=0.5.

ANSWER Q23: The paper's method is different from SIA because STS steers based on a fixed steering direction and an independent Bernoulli(p) draw per token, whereas SIA steers based on a reward-guided method.

ANSWER Q3: They should expect about 32 positions to be steered. STS independently steers each of 128 positions with probability \(0.25\), giving \(128\times0.25=32\) in expectation.

ANSWER Q4: The dependence arises during SAE feature discovery using the positive and neutral contrastive corpora. Their mean feature-activation differences \(\Delta_i\) determine which top-\(K\) decoder directions are selected.

ANSWER Q5: Full steering would likely have shown sharply elevated perplexity and repetition, potentially producing incoherent or repetitive text. That would make sparse steering look artificially favorable by comparing it against an unnecessarily overpowered and degraded full-steering baseline rather than its best fluency-preserving operating point.

ANSWER Q6: The main rationale for SBS would be undermined. SBS treats the leading window as a privileged intervention site specifically because early tokens are assumed to have disproportionate contextual influence.

ANSWER Q7: A given \(\alpha\) would no longer represent a fixed intervention norm. Increasing \(K\) from 10 to 20 could change, and likely increase, the norm of the summed direction, so the same \(\alpha\) would produce a different effective perturbation strength.

ANSWER Q8: Lowering \(p\) reduces the number of displaced token positions, so increasing \(\alpha\) deepens the displacement at each remaining steered position. The displacement analysis therefore treats \(p\) and \(\alpha\) as partly substitutable routes to a similar behavioral shift.

ANSWER Q9: Each generation would be either fully steered at every token or not steered at all. Paper STS instead steers a random subset within each generation, so its realized fraction is usually near \(p\), whereas the altered method’s per-generation fraction would be either 0 or 1.

ANSWER Q10: When the SBS gate fires, it steers every position in the leading window and none after it. Doubling \(W\) from 32 to 64 therefore approximately doubles the number—and hence fraction—of steered tokens for sequences long enough to contain both windows.

ANSWER Q11: It is likely too low. The paper finds that the best-performing \(\alpha\) rises as \(p\) falls, so an \(\alpha\) optimized at \(p=1\) is generally weaker than optimal at \(p=0.3\).

ANSWER Q12: STS at \(p=0.5\) should achieve roughly \(0.285\) or slightly more toxicity reduction, since it recovered over 95% of full steering. This implies that many every-token interventions are redundant for toxicity reduction.

ANSWER Q13: Lowering \(p\) leaves more hidden states unchanged and reduces the aggregate residual-stream displacement from the model’s native activation distribution. This reduces off-manifold drift that can cause high perplexity, incoherence, and repetition.

ANSWER Q14: The comparison uses matched nominal \(p\), not matched realized intervention budgets. Because SBS only steers a bounded leading window, it steers substantially fewer total tokens than STS at the same \(p\), and the paper finds no universal ordering once realized budgets are matched.

ANSWER Q15: It suggests that much of STS’s apparent toxicity advantage at matched nominal \(p\) comes from SBS receiving a smaller realized intervention budget. At nearly matched realized ratios, STS and SBS achieve almost identical reductions, \(0.237\) versus \(0.232\), although STS remains slightly ahead.

ANSWER Q16: The prompting baseline was deliberately developed through iterative prompt engineering on held-out data. The authors tested multiple formulations and retained the coherent prompt that minimized toxicity or maximized target-emotion probability, so it was intended as a strong baseline.

ANSWER Q17: The recovery numbers are likely conservative. Because the optimal \(\alpha\) generally increases as \(p\) decreases, holding it at the \(p=1\) value likely understates what sparse steering could achieve after per-\(p\) tuning.

ANSWER Q18: It shows that SBS can outperform STS on fear when their realized intervention budgets are comparable: SBS gains \(0.092\) versus STS’s \(0.055\) despite a slightly lower realized ratio. Thus STS does not universally dominate SBS at matched budgets.

ANSWER Q19: No. The paper calibrates \(\alpha\) separately for each model and task, choosing 2 for LLaMA toxicity but 35 for Gemma toxicity because their activation spaces and SAEs have different scales and operating points.

ANSWER Q20: No, it would not normally be selected as a target-promoting top feature. Its differential is \(\Delta_i=0.2-0.8=-0.6\), whereas the procedure ranks features by the largest positive target-versus-neutral differential.

ANSWER Q21: Temperature 0.1 produces relatively low-randomness decoding, so the experiments do not establish how independently sampled STS gates interact with more stochastic token sampling. Higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, or other decoding procedures could alter both behavioral effects and fluency.

ANSWER Q22: SBS is more disadvantaged by the fixed \(\alpha\). Its realized ratio is only about 0.13, so the alpha–\(p\) relationship suggests it would need a larger per-token magnitude than STS at a realized ratio near 0.49 to compensate for its much sparser intervention.

ANSWER Q23: SIA uses a different intervention space, training requirement, inference process, and evaluation protocol. It trains and queries a value model, performs logit-space reward-guided selection, and reports reward-model evaluation involving best-of-\(N\) or search, whereas this paper gates a fixed SAE direction and generates one completion.

ANSWER Q24: Perplexity would be expected to rise sharply, from roughly 30 with preservation enabled to roughly 82 without it in the reported ablation. The guards keep steered activations closer to the model’s natural operating regime.

ANSWER Q25: It retains about \(0.237/0.263\approx0.90\), or 90%, of the \(p=0.9\) effect. This supports the main claim that steering substantially fewer tokens can preserve most of the behavioral shift.

ANSWER Q26: STS does not identify behaviorally critical positions. It applies independent, position-agnostic Bernoulli gates, while SIA uses a separately trained value model and related signals to select positions judged important.

ANSWER Q27: No. Even at \(p=1\), SBS steers only positions \(t\leq64\); every later token remains unsteered, so it is not equivalent to full steering for sequences longer than 64 tokens.

ANSWER Q1: Conservative. Because the best-performing alpha rises as p falls, using the smaller p=1-calibrated alpha likely understates the behavioral effect sparse steering could achieve after per-p retuning.

ANSWER Q2: The main rationale for SBS would be substantially weakened. Its leading-window design relies on early tokens having disproportionate influence; without that property, there would be no clear reason to privilege an initial block over other positions.

ANSWER Q3: SBS steers every position within the W-token window whenever its single sequence-level gate fires. Thus, with sequence length and p fixed, doubling W approximately doubles the expected number and realized fraction of steered tokens.

ANSWER Q4: The summary is wrong because STS does not identify critical positions. It independently samples each token’s gate at random, whereas SIA uses a separately trained value model to select behaviorally important positions.

ANSWER Q5: Perplexity would likely rise sharply, from roughly 30 with preservation enabled to about 82 without it. The ablation indicates that the guards keep perturbed activations closer to the model’s natural operating regime.

ANSWER Q6: Generally no: its differential is \(\Delta=0.2-0.8=-0.6\), so it ranks as negatively associated with the target behavior. Strictly, inclusion depends on the other features’ differentials, but it would rank below every feature with \(\Delta>-0.6\).

ANSWER Q7: No. Alpha is calibrated separately for each model and task: toxicity used alpha 2 for LLaMA but 35 for Gemma-2 2B, so alpha 2 would be far below the paper’s Gemma operating point.

ANSWER Q8: SBS is more disadvantaged. At nominal p=0.5 it realizes a much lower intervention ratio than STS, yet both use the same p=1-calibrated alpha even though the paper finds that lower intervention ratios favor larger alpha values.

ANSWER Q9: It is likely too low. The paper finds that the best-performing alpha increases as p decreases, so the optimum at p=0.3 should generally exceed the value calibrated at p=1.

ANSWER Q10: It retains \(0.237/0.263\approx0.90\), or about 90%, of the p=0.9 effect. This supports the main claim that sparse steering can recover most of the behavioral shift while perturbing substantially fewer tokens.

ANSWER Q11: Each generation would be either fully steered at every token or completely unsteered, rather than containing a random mixture of steered and unsteered positions. The average across many sequences would still be p, but sequence-level variance would be much larger.

ANSWER Q12: SIA uses a different intervention space, a trained value model, auxiliary guidance queries, and an evaluation protocol involving reward-model scoring and best-of-N generation. Because these training, inference, and evaluation differences make the numbers noncommensurable, the paper treats SIA as related work rather than a direct baseline.

ANSWER Q13: They should expect lower perplexity and repetition than under full steering. The paper finds both degradation metrics rise monotonically with intervention density, so p=0.4 leaves more activations unperturbed and generally preserves fluency better.

ANSWER Q14: No. At p=1, SBS always steers positions \(t\leq64\), but all positions after the leading 64-token window remain unsteered.

ANSWER Q15: Lowering p reduces the number of positions whose residual-stream states are displaced from their unsteered values. This keeps more of the sequence near the model’s native activation distribution, reducing off-manifold drift that causes high perplexity and repetition.

ANSWER Q16: Full steering would have shown sharply elevated perplexity, repetition, and likely incoherent output because perturbations accumulate at every token. That would make sparse methods look artificially favorable against an intentionally over-strength, poorly calibrated dense baseline.

ANSWER Q17: They should expect \(128\times0.25=32\) steered positions. Each position receives an independent Bernoulli(0.25) gate, so the expected count is 32, although the realized count will vary.

ANSWER Q18: Temperature 0.1 makes decoding relatively deterministic and limits sampling-level variability. It therefore remains unknown whether STS behaves similarly under higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search, or stronger interactions between token sampling and random gates.

ANSWER Q19: The prompting baseline was deliberately optimized through iterative prompt engineering. The authors tested multiple formulations and selected the one performing best on a held-out set while retaining coherent output, rather than using a naive one-line instruction.

ANSWER Q20: The main effectiveness experiments calibrate alpha once under full steering at p=1 and then hold it fixed across every stochastic method and ratio. Thus, the low-p results do not benefit from separate magnitude searches and may actually understate sparse steering’s potential.

ANSWER Q21: Increasing p displaces more token positions, while increasing alpha produces a deeper displacement at each steered position. Because both enlarge the overall target-aligned residual-stream shift, a larger alpha can compensate for intervening at fewer positions.

ANSWER Q22: The nominal p values do not represent equal intervention budgets: SBS steers only a bounded leading window, so it realizes far fewer steered tokens than STS at the same p. The fixed p=1-calibrated alpha also disadvantages this lower-budget SBS condition, and matched-budget results show that the ordering varies by task and operating point.

ANSWER Q23: A given alpha would no longer denote a fixed-magnitude perturbation. Increasing K from 10 to 20 could change the summed vector’s norm substantially, so the same alpha could produce a stronger or weaker residual-stream displacement depending on the added directions’ magnitudes and alignment.

ANSWER Q24: It should achieve more than 95% of 0.30, or roughly at least 0.285 toxicity reduction. This implies that about half the token-level interventions used by full steering are largely redundant in that setting.

ANSWER Q25: At nearly matched realized budgets, their toxicity reductions are essentially equal: 0.237 for STS versus 0.232 for SBS. This suggests much of STS’s apparent advantage at matched nominal p comes from SBS receiving a smaller realized intervention budget, rather than an intrinsic superiority of random token gating.

ANSWER Q26: The dependence arises during contrastive feature discovery. Mean SAE activations on the positive and neutral corpora determine each \(\Delta_i\), which determines the selected top-K features and therefore the final steering direction.

ANSWER Q27: SBS is better in this matched-budget comparison: it gains 0.092 with a slightly lower realized ratio, versus STS’s 0.055. This shows that block steering can be competitive or superior for fear elicitation once realized intervention budgets are approximately equal.

ANSWER Q1: Lowering \(p\) should improve fluency by leaving more token positions undisplaced and keeping the residual stream closer to its native activation distribution. This reduces off-manifold drift that can cause high perplexity, incoherence, and repetition.

ANSWER Q2: They should expect lower perplexity and repetition than under full steering. On Gemma-2 2B toxicity reduction, both metrics increased monotonically with intervention density, so \(p=0.4\) should impose less fluency cost than \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q3: The prompting baseline was deliberately optimized rather than a naive one-line instruction. The authors iterated over formulations on held-out data and retained the prompt that produced the strongest task-specific behavioral effect while remaining coherent.

ANSWER Q4: The sparse-steering recovery numbers are likely conservative. Because the best-performing \(\alpha\) rises as \(p\) falls, using the smaller \(p=1\)-calibrated magnitude likely underpowers sparse settings relative to what per-\(p\) tuning could achieve.

ANSWER Q5: Each generation would be either fully steered or completely unsteered, rather than having approximately a fraction \(p\) of its positions randomly steered. The expected fraction is \(p\) only when averaged across many sequences.

ANSWER Q6: When its single gate fires, SBS steers every position in the fixed leading window and none afterward. Doubling \(W\) from 32 to 64 therefore roughly doubles the number—and hence the realized fraction—of steered tokens for sequences of similar length.

ANSWER Q7: The main rationale for SBS would be undermined. Treating the leading window as a privileged atomic intervention site is motivated specifically by the claim that early tokens have disproportionate influence.

ANSWER Q8: Temperature 0.1 produces relatively low-randomness decoding, so it does not show whether STS behaves similarly under more stochastic or structurally different decoding methods. At higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, or beam search, sampling randomness could interact with the random gates and alter both behavior and fluency.

ANSWER Q9: It would not normally be selected as a target-promoting top feature because its differential is \(\Delta_i=0.2-0.8=-0.6\). The procedure ranks features by high positive activation differential, whereas this feature is more active on neutral examples.

ANSWER Q10: No. The magnitude is calibrated separately for each model and task: toxicity uses \(\alpha=2\) for LLaMA 3.1-8B but \(\alpha=35\) for Gemma-2 2B, reflecting different activation and SAE scales.

ANSWER Q11: Lower \(p\) displaces fewer token positions, while higher \(\alpha\) creates a larger displacement at each position that is steered. Because these are partly substitutable routes to behavioral change, increasing \(\alpha\) can compensate for intervening less often.

ANSWER Q12: SBS is more disadvantaged. Its realized intervention ratio is much lower than STS’s at the same nominal \(p\), so it would generally need a larger compensating \(\alpha\), yet both use the smaller magnitude calibrated at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q13: SBS can be more effective than STS on fear when realized budgets are matched. Here SBS obtains a gain of 0.092 with a slightly lower realized ratio than STS’s 0.055, supporting the paper’s conclusion that no universal ordering holds after budget matching.

ANSWER Q14: Perplexity would likely rise sharply, from roughly 30 with the guards to about 82 without them in the reported ablation. The guards prevent the steered activations from drifting too far from the model’s natural operating regime.

ANSWER Q15: STS does not identify critical positions; it independently selects positions using position-agnostic Bernoulli draws. SIA instead uses learned, reward-derived guidance to select or steer important decoding positions.

ANSWER Q16: It should achieve over \(0.285\) toxicity reduction, since the paper reports recovery of more than 95% at \(p=0.5\). This implies that many of the interventions made by every-token steering are redundant.

ANSWER Q17: Full steering would likely have shown sharply elevated perplexity, repetition, and possibly incoherent output. Comparing sparse methods against such an intentionally oversteered baseline would unfairly favor sparsity because sparse gating would accumulate fewer of the excessive perturbations.

ANSWER Q18: No. At \(p=1\), the gate always fires, but SBS still applies steering only to positions \(t\leq64\); all later tokens remain unsteered.

ANSWER Q19: SIA and this paper use non-comparable intervention and evaluation protocols. SIA trains and queries an auxiliary value model, intervenes in logit space, and uses reward-model scoring and best-of-\(N\) procedures, whereas this paper gates a fixed SAE residual-stream direction and produces one completion.

ANSWER Q20: The dependence arises during SAE feature discovery. Equation 2 computes positive-versus-neutral mean activation differences from the chosen contrastive corpora, so those datasets determine which top-\(K\) features and decoder directions are selected.

ANSWER Q21: It is likely too low for maximizing behavioral effect at \(p=0.3\). The paper consistently finds that the best-performing magnitude increases as the intervention ratio decreases.

ANSWER Q22: The main effectiveness experiments calibrate \(\alpha\) once under full steering at \(p=1\) and hold it fixed for every lower ratio and method. Thus the low-\(p\) results do not benefit from separate magnitude searches.

ANSWER Q23: They should expect \(128\times0.25=32\) steered positions. Each position receives an independent Bernoulli draw with probability 0.25, so 32 is the binomial expectation.

ANSWER Q24: STS retains a small toxicity advantage at approximately matched realized budgets: 0.237 versus 0.232 despite steering a slightly smaller fraction. However, the near equality shows that the much larger differences at matched nominal \(p\) can partly result from SBS realizing a lower token budget.

ANSWER Q25: A given \(\alpha\) would no longer represent a fixed-norm perturbation. Changing \(K\) would change the norm of the summed direction—depending on the added vectors’ magnitudes and alignment—so the effective steering strength could change even with the same \(\alpha\).

ANSWER Q26: It retains \(0.237/0.263\approx0.90\), or about 90%, of the \(p=0.9\) effect. This supports the main claim that sparse steering can recover most of the behavioral shift while intervening at substantially fewer positions.

ANSWER Q27: The comparison does not establish an intrinsic twofold advantage because matched nominal \(p\) does not mean matched realized intervention budget. SBS steers only a bounded early window and is also more underpowered by the fixed \(p=1\)-calibrated \(\alpha\), so method efficiency must be compared at similar realized ratios and can vary by task.

content:
ANSWER Q1: In any single generation, the steering would be all-or-nothing: with probability p every token is steered and with probability 1−p no token is steered, whereas the paper's STS interleaves steered and unsteered positions within one generation. Both have expected steered fraction p, but the altered version has maximal per-sequence variance (it is essentially SBS with W = T) and never mixes dense and sparse intervention within a single completion.

ANSWER Q2: Appendix D.3 shows that p and α are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift: raising p adds more displaced positions, while raising α deepens the displacement at each intervened token. Therefore, when p falls and fewer positions are perturbed, a larger per-token magnitude is needed to reach the same effect, so the best-performing α rises as the ratio falls.

ANSWER Q3: The summary is wrong because STS is explicitly position-agnostic and random — it makes "no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant" and simply samples an independent Bernoulli(p) gate at each position. SIA, by contrast, identifies "critical junctions" using a separately trained value model distilled from trajectory rewards, requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding; STS needs no learned selector, reward model, or position identification.

ANSWER Q4: At nearly identical realized budgets (0.261 vs. 0.287 steered tokens), SBS achieves a substantially larger fear gain (0.092 vs. 0.055), showing the block-level variant is not merely competitive but actually better than STS on fear once budgets are equalized. This means STS's apparent superiority at matched nominal p on fear is largely a budget artifact, consistent with the paper's statement that no single ordering holds once realized budgets are matched.

ANSWER Q5: Temperature 0.1 makes sampling nearly deterministic, so the experiments isolate only gate-level randomness and never test how it interacts with sampling-level randomness. Since the paper uses a single decoding configuration, it is unknown whether the recovery percentages and fluency trade-offs hold under higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, or beam search, leaving the generality of the STS results open.

ANSWER Q6: No. The discovery procedure ranks features by Δᵢ = mean activation on the positive set minus mean activation on the neutral set (Eq. 2), giving Δᵢ = 0.2 − 0.8 = −0.6 for this feature. Because it is more active on the neutral set than on the target-behavior set, it would not rank among the top-K features selected for steering.

ANSWER Q7: The rationale would collapse. SBS's design — treating a leading window of size W as an atomic intervention site — rests entirely on prior findings that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence and that early-token intervention alone can steer behavior; if early tokens were no more influential than later ones, concentrating the intervention on a leading window would be an arbitrary, unmotivated choice.

ANSWER Q8: Because SIA differs from STS in intervention space (logit-space reweighting via a trained value model versus residual-stream addition of a fixed SAE direction), training requirements, inference procedure (best-of-N generation with reward-model scoring), and evaluation protocol. The paper states that given these differences the reported results are not directly commensurable, so it treats SIA as related work rather than an experimental baseline.

ANSWER Q9: The comparison is at matched nominal p, not matched realized budget: at p=0.5, SBS with W=32 steers only about 13% of tokens while STS steers about 49%, so STS is delivering nearly four times the interventions. Appendix D.2 shows that once realized budgets are matched, no single ordering holds across tasks (the block variant is competitive or better on fear), and the finding is also specific to the tested settings, so no intrinsic "twice as effective" factor can be inferred.

ANSWER Q10: No. The paper calibrates α per model and task, selecting α = 2 for LLaMA 3.1-8B on toxicity but α = 35 for Gemma-2 2B on the same task — an order-of-magnitude difference. Reusing α = 2 on Gemma would apply a magnitude far below its calibrated operating point (chosen just below the perplexity/repetition inflection), yielding much weaker steering than the paper's Gemma results.

ANSWER Q11: SBS is more disadvantaged. Since the best-performing α rises as the intervention ratio falls, and SBS (W=32) at nominal p=0.5 realizes only a 0.134 ratio versus STS's 0.492, the single fixed α calibrated at p=1 sits further below SBS's optimal magnitude than below STS's, so SBS would benefit more from a larger α to compensate for its sparser realized intervention.

ANSWER Q12: No. By its definition (Eq. 4), SBS only adds the steering vector at positions t ≤ W and leaves all positions t > W unsteered regardless of the gate. With p=1 the single per-sequence gate fires with certainty, but only the first 64 tokens of a longer sequence receive the signal.

ANSWER Q13: At essentially matched realized budgets (0.492 vs. 0.531), STS achieves slightly higher toxicity reduction (0.237 vs. 0.232), suggesting STS's toxicity advantage is not merely an artifact of nominal-p comparisons. This is consistent with the paper's claim that once budgets are matched, STS retains an advantage on toxicity reduction over much of the range.

ANSWER Q14: The steering-direction discovery step in Section 3.1. The mean activation differential Δᵢ (Eq. 2) is computed between a positive set P and a neutral set N, and the top-K features by Δᵢ are combined into the steering direction, so different contrastive corpora produce different differentials, different selected features, and ultimately a different steering direction.

ANSWER Q15: α would lose comparability across settings. Without unit normalization, the steering signal's actual size becomes α·‖Σvₖ‖, and the summed vector's norm grows roughly with the number of aggregated decoder directions, so the same α value with K=20 would inject substantially more displacement per steered token than with K=10, conflating steering strength with dictionary-aggregation size.

ANSWER Q16: Perplexity would be roughly 82 rather than about 30. The ablation on the Gemma-2 2B toxicity setting (Figure 4) shows that enabling the guards reduces perplexity from approximately 82 to 30 and cuts repetition by roughly a factor of three, so without them generation quality would be markedly worse.

ANSWER Q17: They should expect lower perplexity and lower Rep-3/Rep-4 than full steering. Figure 2 reports this exact setting (Gemma-2 2B, toxicity reduction) and shows degradation grows monotonically with steering density, with full steering at the high end, so operating at p=0.4 sits below the full-steering fluency cost.

ANSWER Q18: SBS steers exactly the fixed leading window of W positions whenever its single per-sequence Bernoulli(p) gate fires, so the expected steered count scales as p·W. Doubling W from 32 to 64 doubles the number of positions steered per firing, and hence roughly doubles the realized ratio at the same p.

ANSWER Q19: Conservative. Because the best-performing magnitude rises as the ratio falls, the fixed α calibrated at p=1 is suboptimal (too small) at lower ratios, so the reported sparse recovery numbers understate what could be achieved with per-p re-tuned magnitudes — the paper explicitly notes the results "do not benefit from any per-p re-tuning of the magnitude."

ANSWER Q20: Too low. The paper's finding in Section 4.3 is that the best-performing α rises as the intervention ratio falls, so at p=0.3 the optimal magnitude exceeds the value that was best at p=1.

ANSWER Q21: Roughly 0.285, since the paper reports STS at p=0.5 recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction on LLaMA 3.1-8B (0.95 × 0.30). This implies that the majority of per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant — about half the tokens can be left unperturbed while retaining nearly the whole behavioral effect.

ANSWER Q22: Lowering p reduces the number of positions whose residual-stream activations are displaced off the model's native manifold — as the paper puts it, p "adds more displaced positions" while α deepens displacement per token. With fewer steered positions, the residual stream stays closer to the distribution of natural activations the model can decode fluently, yielding lower perplexity and less repetition at matched behavioral shift.

ANSWER Q23: The paper calibrates α once under full steering (p=1) and holds it fixed across all methods and ratios for its main effectiveness results, explicitly stating that "the sparsity results reported elsewhere do not benefit from any per-p re-tuning of the magnitude." So there was no per-p magnitude search behind the low-p recovery numbers.

ANSWER Q24: The paper's prompting baselines were built through iterative prompt engineering: for toxicity it tested formulations from simple instructions to structured rule-based prompts and selected the variant with the lowest mean toxicity on held-out prompts, and for emotion it iterated over phrasing, tone, and directiveness. The authors describe these baselines as intentionally strong, best-effort prompts precisely so that surpassing them is a meaningful result.

ANSWER Q25: About 90% (0.237/0.263 ≈ 0.90) of the p=0.9 effect is retained at p=0.5. This directly supports the paper's main claim that steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the dense-steering behavioral effect, i.e., dense every-token intervention is largely redundant.

ANSWER Q26: About 32 positions. Each position's gate is an independent Bernoulli(0.25) draw, so in expectation a fraction p of the T=128 positions receive the steering vector: 0.25 × 128 = 32.

ANSWER Q27: The full-steering baseline would have shown sharply degraded quality — high perplexity and repetitive, incoherent, off-manifold text — since beyond the inflection perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 spike even though behavioral effectiveness saturates. This would make the comparison less fair because sparse methods would appear superior partly because the dense baseline was pushed into a degenerate, unreasonable operating regime rather than being evaluated at its best fluency-preserving point.

ANSWER Q1: The full-steering baseline would have produced visibly degenerate text — sharply higher perplexity and heavy, often unrecoverable repetition. Comparing sparse methods against a collapsed baseline would be a strawman: they would look artificially good on fluency merely because full steering was broken, rather than because sparsity genuinely preserves fluency at a fairly chosen operating point.

ANSWER Q2: Perplexity would be substantially worse (higher). The ablation suggests that on Gemma-2 2B toxicity the guards — particularly clamping/norm preservation, which matter for Gemma-2's large outlier activations — carry a real share of the fluency preservation, so removing them pushes perplexity well above the guarded configuration even before sparsity is considered.

ANSWER Q3: It shows STS's advantage is behavior-dependent. At essentially the same steered-token budget (~26–29%), the block method achieves a noticeably larger fear gain (0.092 vs 0.055), so on fear, concentrating the steering into a contiguous early block is more effective than spreading it randomly across tokens — per-token randomization is not uniformly superior.

ANSWER Q4: Alpha would stop being a clean, K-independent step size. Without unit normalization, the summed decoder vector's norm grows with K, so with K=20 the same alpha would produce a stronger effective push than with K=10, and the alpha calibrated at K=10 would no longer mean the same thing (making cross-K and calibration comparisons invalid).

ANSWER Q5: The SAE feature-discovery step: ranking features by their differential activation between the target-behavior corpus and the neutral corpus and summing the top-K decoder directions. Whichever contrastive corpora are chosen determine which features rank highest, so the resulting steering vector — and thus steering quality — inherits that choice.

ANSWER Q6: Because STS does no position selection at all: it flips an independent Bernoulli(p) coin at every generated token and steers wherever it lands heads, ignoring which tokens matter. SIA steers at attributed/critically-important positions, whereas STS's sparsity is deliberately random and position-agnostic — that is the point of the method.

ANSWER Q7: Too low. The paper finds that the behaviorally optimal alpha rises as p falls (fewer steered tokens need a larger per-token push to accumulate comparable effect), so an alpha tuned at p=1 will under-steer when reused at p=0.3.

ANSWER Q8: The rationale would evaporate. SBS is motivated specifically by the finding that perturbing early tokens has outsized influence over the rest of the generation, so concentrating a limited steering budget in an early block maximizes leverage; if all positions were equally influential, there would be no principled reason to prefer early contiguous blocks, and SBS would lose its distinctive justification.

ANSWER Q9: No. Alpha is calibrated per model and behavior at p=1 by locating the inflection where perplexity and repetition degrade, and Gemma-2 2B's calibrated toxicity alpha is a different value because its residual-stream scales and SAE decoder geometry differ from LLaMA 3.1-8B. Porting alpha=2 to Gemma would sit far from Gemma's operating point — in all likelihood far too weak — so the paper's Gemma results would not be reproduced.

ANSWER Q10: Because SIA's reported numbers come from a different setup — different models, steering directions, behaviors, metrics, and a different notion of "fraction of tokens steered" (SIA steers at selected/attributed positions). The paper only plots methods it ran itself under identical conditions (same model, vector, alpha, decoding, evaluation), so placing SIA's externally reported numbers in the same figure would be an apples-to-oranges comparison; SIA is therefore discussed qualitatively.

ANSWER Q13: They should expect about 32 generated positions to be steered. STS gives each position an independent Bernoulli(0.25) gate, so the expected steered fraction is 0.25 of 128 tokens.
ANSWER Q14: The p=0.5 value retains about 0.237/0.263 ≈ 90% of the p=0.9 effect. This supports the paper’s claim that steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of denser steering.
ANSWER Q15: The inference is flawed because the two methods do not use the same realized intervention budget at the same nominal p; STS steers a much larger fraction of tokens than SBS W=32. Thus the difference confounds per-token randomization with total amount of steering, and matched-budget results show no single intrinsic ordering.
ANSWER Q16: No, because alpha is calibrated per model and task under full steering, and the paper uses alpha=2 for LLaMA toxicity but alpha=35 for Gemma toxicity. A LLaMA value would not produce the same residual displacement or model-specific behavioral/fluency tradeoff on Gemma.
ANSWER Q17: A single generation would be all-or-nothing: either every token is steered or none are. The expected steered fraction would still be p, but the realized pattern would lack STS’s within-generation mixture of steered and unsteered positions.
ANSWER Q18: SBS W=32 is more disadvantaged. Its realized ratio at nominal p=0.5 is much lower, and since the optimal alpha rises as the effective intervention ratio falls, the p=1-calibrated alpha is likely too weak for SBS more than for STS.
ANSWER Q19: They should expect lower perplexity and lower repetition than full steering. Fluency degradation increases with steering density, so p=0.4 steers fewer positions and keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution.
ANSWER Q20: STS at p=0.5 should achieve roughly 0.285 or more toxicity reduction, since it recovers over 95% of the full-steering effect. This implies that most per-token interventions in dense steering are redundant for the behavioral shift.
ANSWER Q21: SBS steers a leading window of W tokens when its gate fires, so the expected number of steered positions is proportional to pW. Doubling W therefore roughly doubles the expected steered fraction and hence the realized ratio.
ANSWER Q22: That alpha is likely too low. The paper finds the best-performing alpha rises as p falls, so the alpha optimal at p=1 is below the alpha that would maximize effect at p=0.3.
ANSWER Q23: The paper explicitly used carefully iterated, task-specific prompting baselines selected on held-out data, not a naive one-line instruction. They were intentionally made strong so that surpassing them is meaningful.
ANSWER Q24: No, not under the stated top-K-by-Delta_i selection, because Delta_i = 0.2 - 0.8 = -0.6. The procedure selects features with the largest positive mean activation differential for the target-behavior set.
ANSWER Q25: No, because SBS applies the signal only to the leading window t <= W. With p=1 the window is always steered, but tokens after position 64 remain unsteered in a longer sequence.
ANSWER Q26: Temperature 0.1 makes sampling randomness small, so the experiments mainly measure gate randomness in a near-greedy regime. It is therefore open whether STS behaves the same under higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, or beam search where sampling noise interacts with the gates.
ANSWER Q27: The displacement analysis says p adds more displaced token positions while alpha deepens the displacement at each steered position. Since these are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, a lower p requires a larger alpha to produce comparable total residual displacement.

ANSWER Q1: The ablation suggests perplexity would likely increase significantly. Removing fluency-preserving guards allows the steering to disrupt the model's next-token prediction more aggressively, leading to higher uncertainty. Therefore, the guards are critical for maintaining fluency while steering.
ANSWER Q2: The analysis explains this by showing that lower p concentrates the steering effect on fewer tokens. To achieve the same behavioral shift with fewer interventions, the residual-stream displacement per steered token must increase, necessitating a higher alpha.
ANSWER Q3: It leaves generality open because temperature 0.1 is highly deterministic, masking how steering interacts with stochastic sampling. If the model is not sampling stochastically, the randomness of the gate selection cannot be tested against the randomness of the generation.
ANSWER Q4: The reported numbers are likely conservative. Since optimal alpha rises as p falls, using the p=1 calibrated value at lower ratios means the steering magnitude is too small to fully recover the behavior.
ANSWER Q5: The protocol rules this out by using a single alpha calibrated at p=1 for all p values in the main results. This ensures the comparison is on matching steering magnitudes rather than optimized ones for each p.
ANSWER Q6: The mechanism is that lowering p reduces the number of tokens steered, minimizing interference with the residual stream's natural flow. This preserves the coherence of unsteered tokens better than high-p steering.
ANSWER Q7: The rationale for SBS would collapse because it relies on early tokens having disproportionate causal influence over the generation. If early tokens are no more influential than later tokens, selecting them specifically offers no advantage.
ANSWER Q8: This inference is flawed because SBS steers blocks of W tokens, while STS steers individual tokens. Comparing per-token gain without normalizing for block width W ignores the different coverage of the two methods.
ANSWER Q9: The fraction retained is approximately 0.90 (0.237 divided by 0.263). This relates to the main claim that STS maintains high effectiveness even at lower p values, demonstrating robustness to sparsity.
ANSWER Q10: This summary is wrong because STS uses independent Bernoulli draws for token gates, not behaviorally critical positions. SIA uses critical positions, whereas STS relies on random selection to achieve sparsity.
ANSWER Q11: This suggests STS has a toxicity advantage at matched nominal p because it achieves similar reduction with a lower realized ratio. STS is more efficient per steered token compared to SBS.
ANSWER Q12: The feature is that SBS steers contiguous blocks of width W. Doubling W doubles the number of tokens steered per block, linearly increasing the realized ratio of steered positions.
ANSWER Q13: That alpha is likely too low. Given that alpha rises as p falls, the alpha calibrated for p=1 is smaller than what is optimal for p=0.3 to maximize effect.
ANSWER Q14: They should expect 32 positions. This is calculated as the total sequence length (128) multiplied by the probability p (0.25).
ANSWER Q15: Training the SAE features on the contrastive corpora creates this dependence. The features are learned to distinguish between contrasted behaviors, so their quality relies on the corpora used.
ANSWER Q16: The baseline would likely show sharp increases in perplexity and repetition. This makes the comparison less fair because the full-steering baseline would fail fluency constraints, inflating the apparent success of STS.
ANSWER Q17: STS at p=0.5 should achieve roughly 0.15 to 0.20 reduction. This implies per-token interventions are less potent than full steering, as they affect a fraction of the generation.
ANSWER Q18: The meaning of alpha would change because it would no longer represent a unit-norm displacement per feature. Increasing K would scale the total displacement, changing the effective magnitude of alpha.
ANSWER Q19: The steering would be all-or-nothing for the entire sequence. Instead of independent draws per token, a single gate determines if the whole sequence is steered, leading to different token-wise distributions.
ANSWER Q20: This shows SBS achieves higher gain with a lower fraction of steered tokens. However, STS steers more tokens (higher ratio) for lower gain, suggesting SBS is more potent per steered position.
ANSWER Q21: The paper declines to put SIA results side by side because SIA uses a different method (SAE features vs steering vectors). Direct comparison would conflate architectural differences with method effectiveness.
ANSWER Q22: They should expect lower perplexity and repetition relative to full steering. Steering fewer tokens (p=0.4) disrupts the residual stream less than full steering, preserving fluency better.
ANSWER Q23: The paper's setup contradicts this because it uses a controlled baseline (e.g., specific prompts or SOTA) rather than a naive instruction. The comparison is designed to be fair against strong baselines.
ANSWER Q24: The procedure would likely include it. The discovery looks for features with high contrast between neutral and target sets, and this feature shows a significant difference (0.6).
ANSWER Q25: Yes, SBS would steer the first W tokens. Since SBS steers blocks of width W, a sequence longer than W will still contain at least one steered block of that size.
ANSWER Q26: No, the user would not expect the Gemma results. Alpha is calibrated to the specific latent space and scale of LLaMA 3.1-8B, which differs from Gemma-2 2B.
ANSWER Q27: STS is more disadvantaged by the fixed alpha at p=0.5. Since alpha rises as p falls, STS uses a lower alpha than optimal for its higher steered fraction, reducing its potential effect.

ANSWER Q1: STS at p=0.5 retains about 90% of the p=0.9 effect (0.237/0.263 ≈ 0.90). This directly supports the paper's central claim that most of the dense-steering behavioral shift is recoverable while steering only a fraction of tokens (realized ratios 0.492 vs 0.869), at lower fluency cost.

ANSWER Q2: The paper rules this out because α is calibrated once under full steering (p=1) and then held fixed across all methods and ratios. Appendix D.1 explicitly states the sparsity results "do not benefit from any per-p re-tuning of the magnitude," so STS's low-p gains cannot come from per-p magnitude search.

ANSWER Q3: No. The procedure selects the top-K features by the mean activation differential Δ_i = (mean on positive set) − (mean on neutral set), which here is 0.2 − 0.8 = −0.6. A feature that fires more strongly on neutral controls than on target-behavior examples has a negative differential and would not rank among the top features chosen to promote the behavior.

ANSWER Q4: Because the two methods are not directly comparable: SIA intervenes in logit space via a separately trained value model, queries that guidance during decoding, and is evaluated with best-of-N generation and reward-model scoring. Given these differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation protocol, the paper treats SIA as related work rather than an experimental baseline.

ANSWER Q5: They should expect both lower perplexity and lower repetition than full steering. The paper's fluency results (Figure 2, on exactly the Gemma 2-2B toxicity setting) show degradation grows monotonically with steering density, with full steering at the high end, because fewer perturbed positions keep the residual stream closer to its native distribution.

ANSWER Q6: The inference is flawed because matched nominal p does not mean matched realized intervention budget: at p=0.5, SBS (W=32) actually steers only ~13% of tokens versus ~49% for STS, so STS receives roughly 3–4 times the intervention. Moreover, at matched realized budgets the paper finds no single ordering—on fear, SBS is competitive or better (Table 1)—and the fixed α calibrated at p=1 further penalizes the sparser SBS.

ANSWER Q7: SBS (W=32) is more disadvantaged. Because the best-performing α rises as the intervention ratio falls, and SBS at nominal p=0.5 realizes a much sparser effective ratio (~0.134) than STS (~0.492), the fixed p=1-calibrated α is much further below SBS's optimum than STS's.

ANSWER Q8: Temperature 0.1 is near-deterministic decoding, so gate randomness is essentially the only stochasticity in the pipeline. ANSWER Q9: The rationale would collapse. SBS is justified precisely by prior findings that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence and that early-token intervention alone can steer behavior; if early tokens were no more influential, the leading window would be an arbitrary subset of positions with no privileged claim as an "atomic intervention site."

ANSWER Q10: No. Even with p=1 (so the single per-sequence gate always fires), SBS applies the steering only to positions t ≤ W; positions t > W are left unsteered by definition. A sequence longer than 64 tokens would have all tokens after position 64 untouched.

ANSWER Q11: The displacement analysis shows that p and α are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift: raising p adds more displaced positions, while raising α deepens the displacement at each intervened token, and the injected direction is aligned with the target feature. Therefore, when p falls (fewer displaced positions), a larger α is needed to recover the effect by deepening per-token displacement.

ANSWER Q12: Lowering p reduces the number of positions whose residual-stream activations are displaced off the model's natural manifold. Since perplexity and repetition grow monotonically with intervention density, fewer displaced positions keep the generation closer to the distribution of natural activations, yielding more fluent, less repetitive text.

ANSWER Q13: At essentially matched realized budgets (0.492 vs 0.531), the toxicity reductions are statistically indistinguishable (0.237±0.030 vs 0.232±0.033). This suggests that the large gap at matched nominal p (0.237 vs 0.108 at p=0.5) largely reflects STS's bigger realized intervention budget rather than intrinsic per-token superiority at this operating point, although the paper notes STS retains an advantage over much of the lower-budget range.

ANSWER Q14: At comparable realized budgets, SBS (W=64) actually achieves a higher fear gain (0.092 at ratio 0.261) than STS (0.055 at ratio 0.287). This shows that on fear elicitation the block-level variant is competitive with—or better than—STS once budgets are equalized, so STS's nominal-p advantage on fear is largely a budget artifact.

ANSWER Q15: Full steering would have shown sharply inflated perplexity and spikes in Rep-3/Rep-4—off-manifold, degenerate generation—making it a crippled baseline. The comparison would then be unfair because sparse methods would look good mainly by being measured against an artificially weakened dense baseline, overstating the true benefit of sparsity.

ANSWER Q16: SBS draws one Bernoulli(p) gate per sequence and, when it fires, steers the entire bounded leading window of W tokens, so the expected number of steered tokens is p·W. Because this is linear in W, doubling the window from 32 to 64 roughly doubles the expected steered tokens and hence the realized ratio (0.134 → 0.261).

ANSWER Q17: Conservative. Since the best-performing α rises as p falls, the fixed p=1-calibrated α under-steers at sparse ratios, so the reported recovery figures (e.g., >95% at p=0.5) likely understate what sparse steering could achieve with per-p re-tuned magnitudes.

ANSWER Q18: No. The paper calibrates α per model and task, and the selected values differ by an order of magnitude: α=2 for LLaMA 3.1-8B toxicity versus α=35 for Gemma-2 2B toxicity. Reusing LLaMA's α=2 on Gemma would apply a far-below-optimal magnitude and would not reproduce the Gemma results.

ANSWER Q19: α would lose its fixed meaning. Because α scales a direction whose norm would now be ||Σv_k|| (which grows with the number and norms of the summed decoder directions), the same numeric α would produce a different effective residual-stream displacement for K=20 than for K=10, so α values would no longer be comparable across feature counts or methods.

ANSWER Q20: About 32 positions (0.25 × 128). STS samples an independent Bernoulli(0.25) gate at each generated position, so in expectation a fraction p of the up-to-128 tokens receives the vector, with the actual count varying binomially per generation.

ANSWER Q21: Each single generation would be either fully steered (with probability p) or entirely unsteered (with probability 1−p), rather than interspersing steered and unperturbed tokens within one sequence. ANSWER Q22: The summary is wrong because STS is explicitly position-agnostic and training-free: it samples i.i.d. random gates and "makes no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant." ANSWER Q23: Too low. The paper's α–p finding says the best-performing magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, so the α that was optimal at p=1 will under-steer at p=0.3 (even though it remains safe for fluency).

ANSWER Q24: The feature-discovery step in Section 3.1. The steering direction is built by computing each feature's mean activation differential Δ_i between a positive set exhibiting the target behavior and a matched neutral set, then selecting the top-K features by Δ_i—so different contrastive corpora yield different differentials, different selected features, and a different steering direction.

ANSWER Q25: Roughly 0.285 or more (over 95% of 0.30), since the paper reports STS at p=0.5 recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction on LLaMA 3.1-8B. This implies that the majority of per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant—about half the positions can be left unperturbed with almost no loss of behavioral effect.

ANSWER Q26: Perplexity would be dramatically higher: the ablation on the Gemma-2-2B toxicity setting shows perplexity rising from roughly 30 with preservation enabled to roughly 82 with it off (with repetition also cut roughly threefold when the guards are on). Without the guards, steering would push activations off the natural manifold, producing much less fluent, more repetitive text.

ANSWER Q27: The paper's setup contradicts this because the prompting baselines were developed through iterative prompt engineering, testing multiple formulations (from simple instructions to structured rule-based prompts) and selecting the variant that achieved the lowest toxicity or highest target-emotion probability on a held-out set while remaining coherent. The authors describe these baselines as "intentionally strong" so that surpassing them is a meaningful result.

ANSWER Q1: A given alpha would no longer mean a fixed intervention strength. ANSWER Q2: Too low. The paper's alpha–p finding is that the optimal alpha rises as p falls (each steered token must compensate for the unsteered gaps), so an alpha calibrated as best at p=1 will under-steer at p=0.3 and will not maximize the behavioral effect there.

ANSWER Q3: Roughly 0.26–0.27, i.e., about 85–90% of the full-steering reduction. This implies per-token interventions are largely redundant: halving the number of steered tokens costs only ~10–15% of the effect, so behavioral impact saturates rather than scaling linearly with how many tokens are steered.

ANSWER Q4: Conservative. Because the optimal alpha rises as p falls, the fixed p=1-calibrated alpha is below the optimum at sparse ratios, so the reported sparse-steering recovery numbers likely understate what sparse steering could achieve with per-ratio re-tuning.

ANSWER Q5: The displacement analysis shows that steering moves the residual stream by a distance proportional to alpha, and the behavioral effect depends on keeping the trajectory displaced. At high p, displacements from consecutive steered tokens accumulate, so a small alpha suffices (and a large one overshoots into fluency damage); at low p the gaps prevent accumulation, so each individual intervention must be larger—and can safely be larger—to maintain the needed displacement.

ANSWER Q6: The paper's prompting baseline was a serious, deliberately engineered one—a detailed, behavior-targeted safety instruction rather than a throwaway one-liner—so the comparison was against a competitive prompt, not a strawman. Steering nevertheless matched or beat it (including on the effect-versus-fluency tradeoff), which a naive single-line instruction could not have guaranteed.

ANSWER Q7: The summary is wrong because STS does not identify critical positions at all. It applies the steering vector to token positions chosen by independent Bernoulli(p) draws—purely random, position-agnostic selection—whereas SIA's contribution is precisely its (training- or importance-based) identification of which positions matter; STS's point is that such identification is unnecessary.

ANSWER Q2: Because SIA's reported numbers come from a different experimental pipeline (different models, corpora, steering-vector construction, and evaluation protocol), so placing them next to the paper's own numbers would be an apples-to-oranges comparison. The paper only plots methods it ran under identical conditions in Figure 1 and cites SIA's 20–80% finding qualitatively instead.

ANSWER Q3: Perplexity would be substantially higher (worse). The ablation indicates that the guards—especially norm preservation and clamping, which stop the steering vector from inflating the residual norm and triggering repetition loops—are what keep perplexity near baseline in that setting, so removing them sharply degrades fluency.

ANSWER Q4: Because alpha was calibrated once, at p=1 under full steering (just below the fluency inflection), and then held fixed at that single value for every sparsity level in the main experiments. No per-p magnitude search was performed, so the low-p results cannot be an artifact of separately tuned magnitudes.

ANSWER Q5: The displacement analysis shows that the behavioral effect tracks how far the residual stream is pushed from its natural trajectory, and with fewer gated tokens the accumulated displacement at fixed alpha is smaller (with unsteered steps letting the trajectory relax back toward the unsteered path). Reaching a comparable displacement with fewer, more widely spaced interventions therefore requires a larger per-token push, so the optimal alpha rises as p falls.

ANSWER Q6: Too low. Since the best-performing alpha increases as p decreases, an alpha chosen for p=1 will under-steer at p=0.3; maximizing the behavioral effect there would call for a larger magnitude.

ANSWER Q7: 0.237/0.263 ≈ 0.90, so roughly 90% of the near-full (p=0.9) effect is retained while steering only about half the tokens. This directly supports the paper's main claim that sparse, randomly gated token steering preserves most of the behavioral effect at a much lower intervention density.

ANSWER Q8: Lowering p reduces how often the residual stream is displaced from its natural trajectory, and unsteered steps let the model return to its own next-token distribution. Because the displacement analysis ties fluency degradation (perplexity, repetition) to the magnitude and frequency of these deviations, sparser gating yields smaller, less persistent perturbations and hence more fluent text.

ANSWER Q9: No. By definition SBS steers a single contiguous block of at most W tokens per sequence, with a per-sequence Bernoulli(p) gate deciding whether the block is applied at all; even at p=1 only the W=64 positions inside the block receive the vector, so tokens beyond the block are never steered.

ANSWER Q10: Temperature 0.1 is nearly greedy, so essentially the only randomness in generation is the steering gate itself. Under higher-temperature sampling, sampling noise and gate randomness would interact (steered vs. unsteered tokens drawing different tokens whose effects compound), and since that regime was never tested, it is unknown whether STS's recovery and fluency findings transfer to standard decoding temperatures.

ANSWER Q11: The paper reports that STS at p=0.5 recovers roughly 80–90% of the full-steering effect, so one would expect a reduction of about 0.24–0.27 rather than 0.30. This implies per-token interventions are largely redundant: about half the token positions can go unsteered with little loss of behavioral effect.

ANSWER Q12: Because STS does no token selection at all—it gates each token independently with a random Bernoulli(p) draw, without identifying which positions matter. The paper's central point is precisely that untargeted random sparsity suffices, in contrast to methods like SIA that search for behaviorally influential tokens.

ANSWER Q13: The feature-discovery step. The steering vector is built from the top-K SAE features chosen by comparing mean activations on the target-behavior corpus against the neutral corpus, so any bias, noise, or mismatch in those contrastive sets changes which features—and hence which direction—get selected.

ANSWER Q14: SBS is more disadvantaged. Its realized steered fraction at nominal p=0.5 is only ~13% versus ~49% for STS, meaning it is effectively far sparser; since the optimal alpha grows as effective sparsity grows, the single fixed alpha calibrated at p=1 is far too weak for SBS at p=0.5 while being nearly appropriate for STS.

ANSWER Q15: About 32 positions (128 × 0.25). Each generated token is independently gated with probability p, so the expected number of steered positions is p times the number of generated tokens (fewer only if generation stops early).

ANSWER Q16: Alpha would stop being a clean measure of steering strength. Without unit-norm normalization, the summed decoder directions have a norm that grows with K, so going from K=10 to K=20 would change the actual perturbation delivered at the same alpha; a given alpha would then correspond to different residual-stream displacement depending on K, breaking calibration and comparability.

ANSWER Q17: At essentially the same realized steered fraction (~0.26 vs ~0.29), SBS achieves a larger fear gain (0.092 vs 0.055). This shows STS's advantage is behavior-dependent: for fear on Gemma-2 2B, concentrating the steering into a contiguous block beats random per-token gating at matched sparsity.

ANSWER Q18: A single generation would be either fully steered at every token or not steered at all, rather than showing the interleaving of steered and unsteered tokens that independent per-token draws produce. The expected fraction across generations is still p, but the intervention becomes all-or-nothing per sequence—losing the local mixing the paper credits for fluency and effect retention—and across-generation variance increases.

ANSWER Q19: They should expect better fluency than full steering: lower perplexity and fewer repetitions. Steering only ~40% of tokens means the residual stream is displaced less often and the model more frequently continues from its own unmodified distribution, which the paper's displacement analysis links directly to reduced degeneration.

ANSWER Q20: The inference is confounded: at the same nominal p the realized steered fractions differ enormously (~49% for STS vs ~13% for SBS), both methods run a fixed alpha calibrated at p=1 that is increasingly too weak as effective sparsity grows (hurting SBS far more), and the ordering even reverses on other behavior/model combinations such as fear on Gemma-2 2B. The 2× figure therefore reflects setup artifacts, not an intrinsic property of per-token randomization.

ANSWER Q1: A given alpha would no longer correspond to a fixed steering magnitude. The effective perturbation is alpha times the norm of the summed decoder directions, so without unit normalization the injected vector's scale grows with K (and with the particular features chosen); going from K=10 to K=20 would make the same alpha a stronger intervention, and alpha values would not be comparable across K, feature sets, or calibrations.

ANSWER Q2: Too low. The paper's alpha–p finding is that the optimal alpha increases as p decreases, so the value that was best at p=1 will under-steer at p=0.3.

ANSWER Q3: Roughly 0.27, since the paper reports STS at p=0.5 retains on the order of 90% of the full-steering effect (e.g., 0.237/0.263 in Table 1). This implies per-token interventions are largely redundant and propagating: steering about half the positions shifts the context enough that unsteered tokens follow, so behavioral change does not require steering every token.

ANSWER Q4: Conservative. Because the optimal alpha rises as p falls, holding alpha at its p=1 value leaves the sparse conditions under-dosed relative to their optima, so the reported recovery fractions likely understate what sparse steering could achieve with per-p alpha tuning.

ANSWER Q5: The displacement analysis shows the sustained shift of the residual stream along the steering direction is driven by how frequently tokens are steered (roughly scaling like alpha × p), because at unsteered positions the model relaxes back toward its natural trajectory. As p falls the persistent displacement shrinks, so a larger per-application alpha is needed to maintain the same effective displacement and hence the same behavioral effect.

ANSWER Q6: The paper's setup contradicts the "naive one-liner" assumption because the prompting baseline was constructed to be strong — the instruction was selected/optimized over multiple candidate phrasings and evaluated under the same prompts and metrics as the steering methods. So STS beating it reflects a genuinely competitive comparison, not a strawman prompt.

ANSWER Q7: STS does not identify behaviorally critical positions at all. It applies the steering vector at positions chosen by independent Bernoulli(p) draws — a uniformly random subset — whereas SIA explicitly searches for important positions; the paper's point is precisely that you don't need to find the critical tokens.

ANSWER Q8: About 32 positions on average (128 × 0.25). STS draws an independent Bernoulli(0.25) gate at each generated position, so the expected count is p times the sequence length, with binomial fluctuation around 32.

ANSWER Q9: Temperature 0.1 makes decoding nearly deterministic, so the experiments probe the random steering gate in a regime with almost no sampling noise. At realistic temperatures the two sources of randomness would interact — steered tokens can push the trajectory into different sampled continuations, changing effect sizes, variance, and fluency — and this regime was never tested, so generalization is open.

ANSWER Q10: The feature-discovery step: SAE features are ranked by their differential mean activation between the contrastive corpora (target-behavior set vs neutral set), and the top-K decoder directions are summed into the steering vector. Different corpora therefore select different features and yield a different steering direction.

ANSWER Q11: The main effectiveness results use a single fixed alpha per model/behavior, calibrated once at p=1 (just below the fluency inflection) and reused unchanged at every sparsity level — no per-p magnitude search. Moreover, by the alpha–p finding that fixed alpha is suboptimal (too low) at small p, so the protocol actually biases against the sparse methods rather than favoring them.

ANSWER Q12: They should expect lower perplexity and less repetition than full steering (better fluency) while retaining most (~90%) of the toxicity reduction.
